text:
By four o’clock, the city had begun putting its unwanted furniture on the curb, as though a flood were an inspection for which one could prepare.

Outside the pharmacy stood an upholstered chair, burned along one side. Its left arm was black, the stuffing exposed; the right retained a pattern of yellow flowers on green stems. An empty coffee cup sat on the seat.

I stopped because the chair appeared dry. Everything else had absorbed the rain.

“Don’t sit there,” a woman said.

The man beside her had made no movement toward sitting. He was repairing an umbrella.

“I wasn’t going to.”

“You looked as if you might.”

His smile acknowledged, perhaps, a long history of sitting in unsuitable places.

They were in their late fifties. She wore a brown raincoat; he wore a quilted jacket. Between them they carried a paper shopping bag, each holding one handle. Neither suggested changing this arrangement.

The umbrella opened with a report that made us all look upward. The woman laughed. They went on.

I followed them.

For eleven years I had prepared inventories of furnished apartments. We recorded presence and condition: six teaspoons; table, damage to rear corner. After the company was sold and my position disappeared, I continued noticing things with an intention no longer attached to a task.

That afternoon, a flood warning had driven me from my apartment to buy batteries, though I owned nothing that took them.

The man held the umbrella too high. The woman kept lowering his wrist with two fingers. At a corner, she took both handles of the bag. He immediately relieved her of it.

Their conversation was inaudible beneath the rain. Occasionally she turned toward him, and he bent to listen.

At the next intersection, an abandoned bus stood with its lights on. A transparent glove drifted along the gutter, repeatedly filling and emptying. The man waited for it to pass before stepping down.

The woman looked back.

I pretended to study the bus schedule, although it faced the opposite direction. She watched without apparent suspicion, then touched the man’s shoulder.

They continued downhill, toward streets the river had begun to occupy.

Outside a narrow brick house, the woman searched her pockets.

“You had them,” he said.

“I know.”

He found the keys in his own pocket. Neither remarked on this.

They went inside.

I sheltered beneath the shoe shop’s awning opposite. Its window bore a handwritten sign: CLOSED DUE TO CONDITIONS.

A lamp came on behind the house’s half-lowered blind. The woman appeared without her raincoat.

Her green blouse was patterned with yellow flowers.

I looked back along the street, although the chair was too far away to see.

Such fabrics existed in enormous quantities. Nevertheless, I remembered precisely where the blackened upholstery had ended and the flowers resumed.

She kept her left side turned away.

The man brought two glasses. She drank, then held hers against her cheek.

Cold water entered my shoes. I stepped onto the ledge beneath the shop window.

Inside, the man unfolded a pink towel from the shopping bag and laid it over a chair I couldn’t see. The woman sat, disappearing below the blind.

“Waiting for someone?” a passing cyclist asked.

“Yes.”

“You should call them.”

I checked my phone. My sister had sent two messages asking whether I was all right. I typed Yes and watched it fail to send.

Across the street, the man raised the blind and examined the water. Then he left the room.

The woman was fully visible now, sitting upright. Her right hand rested on her knee. Her left arm lay along the chair.

That sleeve was dark.

It might have been wet, or shadowed. I could see it as either, provided I didn’t look directly at it.

She turned toward me without surprise.

I raised a hand.

She did not raise hers.

I thought of knocking, offering to carry things upstairs. There would be an ordinary hallway, an ordinary smell. She would stand, and her sleeve would prove to be dark green.

The man returned carrying a saucepan. He knelt beside her and wrung a cloth into it. The falling water looked black.

He wiped her left arm, supporting her wrist. She watched with restrained annoyance, as though he were removing a stain from her coat.

Then she looked toward me.

He followed her gaze.

I stepped backward off the ledge and nearly fell. When I recovered, the blind was down.

At last I crossed the street, moving sideways against the current, holding a parked car and then the house’s brickwork. Water pressed through a ventilation grille.

I knocked.

Behind the door came the slow scrape of furniture.

“Do you need help?”

The scraping stopped. The man spoke too softly for me to understand.

Then the woman said, clearly, “He’s still there.”

A narrow stream emerged beneath the door. It carried pale scraps that broke apart when I touched them.

I went uphill, holding railings where I could.

Near the pharmacy, the burned chair had shifted off the curb. The cup was gone. Water lifted one side and set it down again.

The damage was worse than I remembered. Its left arm had burned to the wooden frame. A strip of green fabric hung loose, yellow flowers intact along its edge.

I wanted urgently to put it upright.

I gripped the back. It was heavy now, saturated, and the fabric came away in my hand.

For a moment I held it. Then I folded it once, and once again, and put it in my pocket.
